This was added through [[Special:MassEditRegex]] to all pages with the category so apologies if it was just some kind of an error like the image parameter being in Japanese[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 06:00, 27 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox ancient site|type = [[Zenpokoenfun]] | name= Sengenyama Kofun | location= {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, Chiba Prefecture, Ryūkakuji area | coordinates={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E|map_size:10000}} | type= {{ill|Keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} | area= Kofun length approx. 78 meters; including the surrounding ditch, total length approx. 93 meters | burial= {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}, schist sarcophagus, lacquered wooden coffin | built= Early 7th century | Interred_individual= Possibly {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}} (related to the Oomi clan) | burial goods= Gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, gilded and silver openwork fittings, {{ill|Tachi|ja|直刀|12=draft}}, gold-decorated ceremonial bows, gilded harness fittings, iron harnesses, lamellar armor, axes, knives, iron arrowheads, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土希器|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須惧器|12=draft}}, iron nails, lacquer fragments | Historic_site= Designated as a National Historic Site of Japan | Tangible_cultural_properties= burial goods Historic Site1 as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture | image=[[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun1.JPG|250px]]
Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|12=draft}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|12=draft}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|12=draft}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|12=draft}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|12=draft}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|12=draft}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|12=draft}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|12=draft}} sourced from the area around {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|筑波山|12=draft}}, the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as {{ill|Takamatsuzuka Kofun|ja|高松塚古墳|12=draft}}. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|12=draft}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|12=draft}} robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器|1=Sue pottery|12=draft}} from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No {{ill|haniwa|ja|埴輪|12=draft}} or {{ill|fukiishi|ja|葺石|12=draft}} were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|ja|ヤマト王権|12=draft}} or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墳群|12=draft}} saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Temple|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|12=draft}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|12=draft}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|12=draft}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of {{ill|Lake Katori|ja|香取海|12=draft}}, a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kashima Jingū|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft}}. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|12=draft}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|12=draft}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|12=draft}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichirō|ja|白石太一郎|12=draft}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|12=draft}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|12=draft}}, 2000. Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|12=draft}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|12=draft}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|12=draft}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|12=draft}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|12=draft}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|12=draft}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|12=draft}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|12=draft}} sourced from the area around {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|筑波山|12=draft}}, the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as {{ill|Takamatsuzuka Kofun|ja|高松塚古墳|12=draft}}. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|12=draft}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|12=draft}} robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器|1=Sue pottery|12=draft}} from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No {{ill|haniwa|ja|埴輪|12=draft}} or {{ill|fukiishi|ja|葺石|12=draft}} were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|ja|ヤマト王権|12=draft}} or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墳群|12=draft}} saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Temple|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|12=draft}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|12=draft}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|12=draft}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of {{ill|Lake Katori|ja|香取海|12=draft}}, a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kashima Jingū|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft}}. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|12=draft}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|12=draft}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|12=draft}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichirō|ja|白石太一郎|12=draft}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|12=draft}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|12=draft}}, 2000. Please do not use any bots that just remove the unknown parameters without looking at them. This was added through [[Special:MassEditRegex]] to all pages with the category so apologies if it was just some kind of an error like the image parameter being in Japanese[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 06:00, 27 March 2025 (UTC)}} {{Infobox ancient site|type = [[Zenpokoenfun]] | name= Sengenyama Kofun | location= {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, Chiba Prefecture, Ryūkakuji area | coordinates={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E|map_size:10000}} | type= {{ill|Keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} | area= Kofun length approx. 78 meters; including the surrounding ditch, total length approx. 93 meters | burial= {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}, schist sarcophagus, lacquered wooden coffin | built= Early 7th century | Interred_individual= Possibly {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}} (related to the Oomi clan) | burial goods= Gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, gilded and silver openwork fittings, {{ill|Tachi|ja|直刀|12=draft}}, gold-decorated ceremonial bows, gilded harness fittings, iron harnesses, lamellar armor, axes, knives, iron arrowheads, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土希器|12=draft}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須惧器|12=draft}}, iron nails, lacquer fragments | Historic_site= Designated as a National Historic Site of Japan | Tangible_cultural_properties= burial goods Historic Site1 as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture | image=[[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun1.JPG|250px]]
Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|12=draft}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|12=draft}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|12=draft}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|12=draft}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|12=draft}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|12=draft}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|12=draft}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|12=draft}} sourced from the area around {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|筑波山|12=draft}}, the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as {{ill|Takamatsuzuka Kofun|ja|高松塚古墳|12=draft}}. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|12=draft}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|12=draft}} robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器|1=Sue pottery|12=draft}} from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No {{ill|haniwa|ja|埴輪|12=draft}} or {{ill|fukiishi|ja|葺石|12=draft}} were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|ja|ヤマト王権|12=draft}} or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墳群|12=draft}} saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Temple|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|12=draft}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|12=draft}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|12=draft}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of {{ill|Lake Katori|ja|香取海|12=draft}}, a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kashima Jingū|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft}}. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|12=draft}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|12=draft}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|12=draft}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichirō|ja|白石太一郎|12=draft}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|12=draft}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|12=draft}}, 2000. Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Sakae, Chiba|ja|栄町|12=draft}}, within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|12=draft}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|12=draft}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|12=draft}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|12=draft}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|12=draft}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|12=draft}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|12=draft}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|12=draft}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|12=draft}} sourced from the area around {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|筑波山|12=draft}}, the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as {{ill|Takamatsuzuka Kofun|ja|高松塚古墳|12=draft}}. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|12=draft}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a {{ill|Heian period|ja|平安時代|12=draft}} robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須恵器|1=Sue pottery|12=draft}} from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No {{ill|haniwa|ja|埴輪|12=draft}} or {{ill|fukiishi|ja|葺石|12=draft}} were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|ja|ヤマト王権|12=draft}} or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墳群|12=draft}} saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Temple|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|12=draft}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|12=draft}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|12=draft}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of {{ill|Lake Katori|ja|香取海|12=draft}}, a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at {{ill|Katori Jingū|ja|香取神宮|12=draft}} and {{ill|Kashima Jingū|ja|鹿島神宮|12=draft}}. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|12=draft}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|12=draft}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|12=draft}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichirō|ja|白石太一郎|12=draft}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|12=draft}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|12=draft}}, 2000. ISBN 4-250-20410-3. *** Hirose Kazuo, "Transtypeation of the Yamato Kingship." * The 10th {{ill|Tōhoku-Kantō Keyhole-shaped Kofun Research Meeting|ja|東北·関東前方後円墟研究会|12=draft}}, *Post-Keyhole-shaped Kofun and the End of Tumuli*, Summary Materials, 2005. *** Kurita Norihisa, "Post-Keyhole-shaped Kofun and the End of Tumuli in Chiba Prefecture." * Edited by Sasaki Ken’ichi, *Archaeological Reader 12: Late-Stage Kofun Groups in Kantō*, Rokuichi Shobō, 2007. ISBN 978-4-947743-55-8. *** {{ill|Wada Seigo|ja|和田智谷|12=draft}}, "Analytical Perspectives on Kofun Groups and Clustered Kofuns." *** Ōta Hiroyuki, "Trends of Late-Stage Kofun in Northern Musashi." *** Hagiwara Kyōichi, "Late-Stage Clustered Kofuns in the Shimōsa Region." *** Kawashiri Akinari, "A Perspective on the 7th-Century Eastern Provinces." * Edited by {{ill|Yoshimura Takehiko|ja|吉村武彦|12=draft}} and {{ill|Yamaji Naomitsu|ja|山路直充|12=draft}}, *Bōsō and Ancient Royal Authority*, Koshi Shoin, 2009. ISBN 978-4-86215-054-7. *** Shirai Kumiko, "From Keyhole-shaped Kofun to Square-shaped Tumuli." *** {{ill|Ōtsuka Hatsushige|ja|大塚初重|12=draft}}, "What Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun Tell Us About the Kofun built." *** Yamaji Naomitsu, "The Establishment of Temples and Their Background." *** Ōkawara Ryūichi, "Inba no Kunikō and the Formation of Administrative Districts." * {{ill|Shiraishi Taichirō|ja|白石太一郎|12=draft}}, *The Wa Kingdom as Seen Through Archaeology*, {{ill|Aoki Shoten|ja|青木書店|12=draft}}, 2009. ISBN 978-4-250-20912-3. * Eastern Provinces Kofun Research Symposium, *The Disappearance of Keyhole-shaped Kofun in the Eastern Provinces*, Summary Materials, 2009. *** Tanaka Hiroshi, "The Disappearance of Keyhole-shaped Kofun in Chiba Prefecture." * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Mura|ja|千葉県立房繁の村|12=draft}}, *The Establishment of Ryūjo: Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group and Ryūkaku-ji Temple*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Mura, 2009. *** Kamino Kiyoshi, "The Tombs of Inba no Kunikō." == See Also == * [[List of Kofun in Japan]] * [[List of Historic Sites in the Kantō Region]] * {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国連|12=draft}} * {{ill|Ryūkaku-ji|ja|龍角寺|12=draft}} == notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == External Links == * [https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/bsys/index National Historic Site Database] * [http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Education: Additional Historic Site s and name Changes] * [http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/0900305_6.pdf 2008 designation1 designation1s -
