including the surrounding ditch, total length approx. 93 meters | burial= {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, schist sarcophagus, lacquered wooden coffin | built= Early 7th century | Interred_individual= Possibly {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (related to the Oomi clan) | burial goods= Gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, gilded and silver openwork fittings, [[:en:Chokutō|Tachi]], gold-decorated ceremonial bows, gilded harness fittings, iron harnesses, lamellar armor, axes, knives, iron arrowheads, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土希器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haji pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須惧器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sue pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, iron nails, lacquer fragments | Historic_site= Designated as a National Historic Site of Japan | Tangible_cultural_properties= burial goods Historic Site1 as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture | image=[[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun1.JPG|250px]]
Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped tumulus|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} located in [[:en:Sakae, Chiba|Sakae, Chiba]], within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 竹葉山真邦}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haniwa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofungun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji]] in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asuka period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/phyllite|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 結晶片岩}} sourced from the area around [[:en:Mount Tsukuba|Mount Tsukuba]], the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as [[:en:Takamatsuzuka Tomb|Takamatsuzuka Kofun]]. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|qq=}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]] from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No [[:en:Haniwa|haniwa]] or [[:en:Fukiishi|fukiishi]] were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the [[:en:Yamato Kingship|Yamato Kingship]] or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the [[:en:Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster]] saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji Temple]] was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbanuma Marsh|qq=}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba no Kunikō|qq=}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofun Group|qq=}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of [[:en:Katori Sea|Lake Katori]], a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Jingū]] and [[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingū]]. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Habu District Office|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]]. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichiro|ja|白石太一郎|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraishi Taichirō|qq=}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūzankaku|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, 2000. including the surrounding ditch, total length approx. 93 meters | burial= {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, schist sarcophagus, lacquered wooden coffin | built= Early 7th century | Interred_individual= Possibly {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (related to the Oomi clan) | burial goods= Gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, gilded and silver openwork fittings, [[:en:Chokutō|Tachi]], gold-decorated ceremonial bows, gilded harness fittings, iron harnesses, lamellar armor, axes, knives, iron arrowheads, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土希器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haji pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須惧器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sue pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, iron nails, lacquer fragments | Historic_site= Designated as a National Historic Site of Japan | Tangible_cultural_properties= burial goods Historic Site1 as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture | image=[[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun1.JPG|250px]]
Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped tumulus|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} located in [[:en:Sakae, Chiba|Sakae, Chiba]], within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 竹葉山真邦}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haniwa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofungun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji]] in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asuka period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/phyllite|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 結晶片岩}} sourced from the area around [[:en:Mount Tsukuba|Mount Tsukuba]], the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as [[:en:Takamatsuzuka Tomb|Takamatsuzuka Kofun]]. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|qq=}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]] from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No [[:en:Haniwa|haniwa]] or [[:en:Fukiishi|fukiishi]] were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the [[:en:Yamato Kingship|Yamato Kingship]] or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the [[:en:Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster]] saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji Temple]] was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbanuma Marsh|qq=}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba no Kunikō|qq=}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofun Group|qq=}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of [[:en:Katori Sea|Lake Katori]], a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Jingū]] and [[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingū]]. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Habu District Office|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]]. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichiro|ja|白石太一郎|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraishi Taichirō|qq=}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūzankaku|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, 2000. including the surrounding ditch, total length approx. 93 meters | burial= {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}, schist sarcophagus, lacquered wooden coffin | built= Early 7th century | Interred_individual= Possibly {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (related to the Oomi clan) | burial goods= Gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, gilded and silver openwork fittings, [[:en:Chokutō|Tachi]], gold-decorated ceremonial bows, gilded harness fittings, iron harnesses, lamellar armor, axes, knives, iron arrowheads, {{ill|Haji pottery|ja|土希器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haji pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Sue pottery|ja|須惧器|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sue pottery|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, iron nails, lacquer fragments | Historic_site= Designated as a National Historic Site of Japan | Tangible_cultural_properties= burial goods Historic Site1 as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture | image=[[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun1.JPG|250px]]
Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped tumulus|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} located in [[:en:Sakae, Chiba|Sakae, Chiba]], within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 竹葉山真邦}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haniwa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofungun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji]] in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asuka period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/phyllite|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 結晶片岩}} sourced from the area around [[:en:Mount Tsukuba|Mount Tsukuba]], the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as [[:en:Takamatsuzuka Tomb|Takamatsuzuka Kofun]]. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|qq=}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]] from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No [[:en:Haniwa|haniwa]] or [[:en:Fukiishi|fukiishi]] were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the [[:en:Yamato Kingship|Yamato Kingship]] or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the [[:en:Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster]] saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji Temple]] was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbanuma Marsh|qq=}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba no Kunikō|qq=}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofun Group|qq=}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of [[:en:Katori Sea|Lake Katori]], a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Jingū]] and [[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingū]]. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Habu District Office|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]]. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichiro|ja|白石太一郎|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraishi Taichirō|qq=}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūzankaku|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, 2000. Sengenyama Kofun mound
The right side is the front part, and the left is the rear circular part | map= {{location map|Japan Chiba|coordinates=35|coordinates=49|coordinates=40|lon_deg=140|lon_min=16|lon_sec=09|map_dot_label=Sengenyama Kofun|mark=前方後円墟-南西.svg|marksize=25|caption=location in Chiba Prefecture|position=bottom|width=200|float=center}} {{maplink2|type=point|frame=yes|plain=yes|zoom=14|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{Coord|35|49|40|N|140|16|09|E}}}} }} '''Sengenyama Kofun''' (浅間山古墟) is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped tumulus|ja|前方後円墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped tumulus|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} located in [[:en:Sakae, Chiba|Sakae, Chiba]], within the {{ill|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|ja|龍角寺古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster). Constructed in the early 7th century, it is the largest tumulus within the cluster and a Historic Site1 National Historic Site of Japan. == Overview == The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, to which Sengenyama Kofun belongs, was first constructed in the second quarter of the 6th century during the late {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墟時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. To date, dd4 tumuli have been confirmed within the cluster[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html "Chiba Education: Additions and name Changes to National Historic Sites"]. Sengenyama Kofun, with a mound length of approximately 78 meters, is the largest keyhole-shaped tumulus in the clusterHagiwara (2007), pp. 127–129. The burial facility within Sengenyama Kofun consists of a multi-chambered {{ill|Yokoana stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokoana stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}} constructed with schist slabs sourced from the {{ill|Mount Tsukuba|ja|竹葉山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Tsukuba|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 竹葉山真邦}} region. Excavations revealed burial goods such as gilded crown decorations, silver crowns, and gilded harness fittingsShirai (2009), pp. 17–21; Ōtsuka (2009), pp. 33–37. No {{ill|Haniwa|ja|執珊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haniwa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} were discovered at the site, confirming its status as one of the latest keyhole-shaped tumuli. The tumulus construction is generally dated to the late 6th to early 7th century, although some researchers propose a more recent timeframe in the second quarter of the 7th centuryTanaka (2009), pp. 87–89. The unique features of the tumulus and its burial goods continue to provoke discussions about the end of the keyhole-shaped tumuli tradition in JapanShirai (2009), p. 365; Tanaka (2009), p. 82. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster was likely constructed under the leadership of the {{ill|Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|ja|印泥国連|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba Kuni no Miyatsuko|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, a regional ruler. Before the construction of Sengenyama Kofun, the nearby {{ill|Kozuhara Kofungun|ja|公津原古墟群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofungun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} was the center of local power. However, after the late 6th century, the Ryūkakuji rulers gained dominance, constructing Sengenyama Kofun as a symbol of their authority. This was followed by the construction of the enormous {{ill|Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|ja|龍角寺岩屋古墟|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkakuji Iwaya Kofun|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, one of Japan’s largest square tumuli, and the establishment of [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji]] in the late 7th centuryKurita (2005), pp. 158–162; Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The Ryūkakuji Kofun Cluster, including Sengenyama Kofun, provides critical insights into the role of regional rulers from the late Kofun period to the {{ill|Asuka period|ja|飛鴨時代|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asuka period|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. The cluster was Historic Site1 as a National Historic Site in 2009, and the burial goods were recognized as tangible cultural properties of Chiba Prefecture. == burial and Layout == [[File:Ryukakuzi-sengenyamakohun2.JPG|thumb|200px|The circular part of Sengenyama Kofun with a shrine at the top]] In 1994, surveys revealed that the mound, previously estimated at 66 meters, was originally about 78 meters in length. As characteristic of late-period keyhole-shaped tumuli, the front part is more developed than the rear circular part, although the front is somewhat shorter than usual. The mound is surrounded by a 7–8 meter wide, 1.3-meter-deep ditch, except on the northwest side, where the terrain was likely flatShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Ishibashi (2002), pp. 24–27. The mound is a three-tiered structure, with the first and second tiers being lower and the third tier higher. The height of the front part is approximately 7 meters, and the rear circular part is about 6.7 meters, suggesting they were originally of equal heightShirai (2002), pp. 21–28; Hagiwara (2002), p. dd7. A multi-chambered stone chamber, entered from the south side of the rear circular part, measures 6.68 meters in length, with a maximum width of 2.34 meters and a height of 2.01 meters. Constructed using large schist slabs from the Mount Tsukuba area, the chamber is divided into a passageway, an antechamber, and a burial chamber. The schist was likely transported via waterways from the Katori Sea regionShirai (2000), p. 69. The antechamber’s entrance was paved with small stones, while schist slabs were used for the other floors. Walls were coated with white clay, but no murals were discoveredShirai (2002), pp. 29–34. == burial and burial goods == The burial facilities and burial goods of Asamayama Kofun, along with the unique discovery of relics, have sparked significant debate. === burial === The rear chamber of the horizontal stone chamber in Asamayama Kofun contains a stone coffin constructed using {{ill|phyllite|ja|片岩|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/phyllite|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 結晶片岩}} sourced from the area around [[:en:Mount Tsukuba|Mount Tsukuba]], the same material used for the chamber itself. The interior of the stone coffin also features a white clay coating similar to that found in the stone chamber. However, the coffin was found largely empty, with no burial goods or skeletal remains detected.Shirai, "burial" (2002), pp. 34–36; Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 49. It is believed that the rear chamber, where the coffin was located, was minimally affected by looting, suggesting the coffin was originally empty for some unknown reason rather than emptied by robbers.Kawashiri (2001), p. 9. Based on the discovery of burial goods and lacquer coatings, it is likely that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed in the antechamber. The lacquer used in the coffin was of relatively low quality, appearing to be unrefined lacquer directly applied to the wood. Although lacquered coffins were used in several tombs from the late 6th to 7th centuries, most examples are found in tumuli of prominent figures in the Kinai region, such as [[:en:Takamatsuzuka Tomb|Takamatsuzuka Kofun]]. In the Kanto region, the only other example is the {{ill|Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyoda)|lt=Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|ja|八幡山古墳 (行田市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hachimanyama Kofun (Gyōda)|qq=}} in Gyōda City, Saitama Prefecture, making Asamayama Kofun a rare and valuable case.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), p. 198. === Artifact Discovery === The discovery of burial goods at Asamayama Kofun exhibits notable characteristics. Iron fragments, including small armor plates, pieces of swords, and fragments of iron horse gear, were found atop the ceiling stones of the passageway. These burial goods were likely displaced by the roots of a cedar tree that grew atop the ceiling stones. While it is possible these burial goods were placed during the burial, the fragmented condition suggests they may have moved from the forecourt due to the tree roots.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 40. The most distinctive finding is the large quantity of burial goods discovered in the forecourt area in front of the passageway. These burial goods were stratified into two layers: the upper layer contained fragments of iron horse gear and swords, likely looted from the stone chamber during a [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] robbery. Mid-Heian period oil lamps used by the looters were also found in this layer, suggesting artifact selection occurred on-site.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 40–45. The lower layer of the forecourt yielded a wealth of burial goods, including gilt bronze horse gear, silver decorative fittings, earrings, iron horse gear, and iron arrowheads. Most of the significant burial goods from Asamayama Kofun, aside from crowns, were recovered from this layer. These items are unlikely to have been displaced by Heian-period looters and may have been moved shortly after the original burial.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 45. Some researchers suggest they were intentionally buried in the forecourt during the original interment.Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Additionally, [[:en:Sue pottery|Sue pottery]] from the mid- to late 7th century, produced in the Tokai region, was found in the forecourt, possibly left in place from the initial burial. burial goods from the antechamber were found primarily on or near the floor stones. Items included gilt bronze and iron horse gear, openwork gilt bronze fittings, iron armor plates, nails, and lacquer remnants, supporting the hypothesis that a lacquered wooden coffin was placed there. Some gilt bronze horse gear near the back of the chamber appears to have remained in its original location, while other items were likely moved shortly after burial. Evidence of human interference includes deliberate backfilling of the chamber with soil, also observed in the rear chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 45–46; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. The rear chamber contained soil deposits when excavated. These deposits, likely introduced after the stone coffin's burial, contained burial goods concentrated in two layers. The upper layer yielded swords and gilt bronze fittings, while the lower layer contained decorative gilt bows, earrings, gilt bronze crown ornaments, and a silver crown.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), pp. 48–49; Tanaka (2009), p. 89. Since the Heian-period robbery, no evidence suggests human entry into the stone chamber.Shirai, "Discovery Status of burial goods" (2002), p. 46. The chamber's partial backfilling and artifact displacement during the robbery complicate the assessment of its funerary goods. No [[:en:Haniwa|haniwa]] or [[:en:Fukiishi|fukiishi]] were found on the tumulus, suggesting Asamayama Kofun represents a late-stage keyhole-shaped kofun.Shirai, "Kofun type and Surrounding Moat" (2002), p. 24. === burial goods === burial goods excavated from Asamayama Kofun include gilt bronze crown ornaments, a silver crown, gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings, swords, decorated bows with gilt details, iron arrowheads, iron armor, gilt bronze and iron horse gear, knives, axes, and Sue pottery. While the items reflect a typical assemblage of kofun-period grave goods, the gilt bronze crown ornaments, silver crown, and gilt bronze horse gear date to the early 7th century. The gilt bronze and silver openwork fittings show Buddhist artistic influences from the same period. The most recent artifact, Sue pottery from the forecourt, dates to the mid- to late 7th century.Shirai, "Summary and Chronological Context" (2002), pp. 198–199; Shiraishi (2002), pp. 200–201; Shirai (2009), p. 21; Ōtsuka (2009), p. 37. The gilt bronze crown ornaments and silver crown suggest connections between the burial individual and the [[:en:Yamato Kingship|Yamato Kingship]] or powerful clans in the Kinai region. The gilt bronze horse gear, found along routes to the Kanto and Tōhoku regions, supports the idea that the deceased held significant importance in the Yamato Kingship.Shirai, "burial goods" (2002), p. 159; Shirai (2009), p. 27. == Relationship with Ryūkaku-ji == [[File:Ryukakuzi-keidai1.JPG|thumb|200px|Ryūkaku-ji precincts]] After the construction of Asamayama Kofun, the [[:en:Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster|Ryūgakuji Kofun Cluster]] saw the creation of the Iwaya Kofun, one of Japan’s largest square-shaped tumuli. Subsequently, during the mid- to late 7th century, [[:en:Ryūkaku-ji|Ryūkaku-ji Temple]] was constructed to the north of the tumulus. It is believed that the local chieftain who ruled the area around {{ill|Inbanuma Marsh|ja|印旛沼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbanuma Marsh|qq=}}, identified as the {{ill|Inba no Kunikō|ja|印波国造|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inba no Kunikō|qq=}}, commissioned the construction of both Asamayama Kofun and Ryūkaku-ji Temple.Yamaji (2009), pp. 93–96; Ōkawara (2009), pp. 315–317. The chieftain responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group replaced the leaders of the earlier {{ill|Kozuhara Kofun Group|ja|公津原古墳群|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kozuhara Kofun Group|qq=}}, who had previously played a leading role in the region. Instead, they constructed monumental tumuli such as Asamayama Kofun and Iwaya Kofun, which became symbols of regional prominence. The Inba no Kunikō is thought to have strengthened their power by controlling the key transportation hub of [[:en:Katori Sea|Lake Katori]], a critical water route connecting Shimōsa to Hitachi and onward to the Tōhoku region. The placement of the later Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group’s tumuli, oriented northeast toward Lake Katori rather than toward Inbanuma Marsh, reflects this strategic emphasis.Shirai (2009), pp. 4–7, 26–27; Yamaji (2009), pp. 104–105. It has also been suggested that the construction of Ryūkaku-ji Temple coincided with the building of the shrine halls at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Jingū]] and [[:en:Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingū]]. This suggests that the Yamato Kingship prioritized the transportation routes through Lake Katori to Hitachi and the Tōhoku region.Yamaji (2009), pp. dd0–dd2. The chieftain, believed to have been responsible for the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group, likely strengthened ties with the Yamato Kingship by controlling these critical transportation routes, as evidenced by the power symbolized in Asamayama Kofun. Additionally, near the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group lies the Ōhata Archaeological Site, believed to be the remains of the {{ill|Habu District Office|ja|埴生郡衙|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Habu District Office|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. This site suggests that the leaders who constructed the Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group maintained their influence as district governors after the establishment of the [[:en:Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]]. This indicates the enduring significance of Asamayama Kofun as a turning point in the history of the region.[http://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/houdou/08dd25.html Chiba Prefecture Education - Regarding the Additional designation1 and name Change of National Historic Sites], Kurita (2005), p. 159; Shirai (2009), pp. 26–27. == References == * {{ill|Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|ja|千葉県立房繁風土記の丘|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group Survey Report*, Chiba Prefectural Bōsō no Fudoki no Oka, 1982. * {{ill|Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|ja|千葉県史料研究財団|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chiba Prefecture Historical Research Foundation|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, *Chiba Prefecture History Research, No. 4*, Chiba Prefecture, 1996. *** {{ill|Shiraishi Taichiro|ja|白石太一郎|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shiraishi Taichirō|qq=}} et al., "Survey Report on Asamayama Kofun, Sakae Town, Inba District." * Shirai Kumiko, "{{ill|Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|ja|龍角寺古墟組|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryūkaku-ji Kofun Group|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}," *Quarterly Archaeology, No. 71*, {{ill|Yūzankaku|ja|雨山閣|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūzankaku|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, 2000.
